screens.title: Operational Insights and Troubleshooting with AWS Systems Manager
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll explore AWS Systems Manager — a unified set of capabilities that help you manage and troubleshoot EC2 instances and on-premises servers at scale. Systems Manager brings together secure interactive access, remote command execution, automated patching, and centralized operational views so you can shorten time-to-resolution and maintain compliance across many instances. You will learn why having the SSM Agent and correct IAM role is a prerequisite, how Session Manager removes the need for SSH keys and open inbound ports, and how Run Command and Patch Manager let you perform repeatable operations safely across a fleet. We’ll also cover Explorer and OpsCenter, which aggregate operational data and surface actionable work items. As you follow this module, think about a fleet you manage: replacing ad-hoc SSH troubleshooting with Session Manager and centralized runbooks reduces risk and creates an audit trail. By the end you'll know which Systems Manager capability to choose for common operational tasks, how to limit blast radius with MaxConcurrency and MaxErrors, and how to keep systems patched in a maintenance window. Which operational pain point would you solve first with Systems Manager?

screens.title: What is AWS Systems Manager (SSM)?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Systems Manager is a suite of capabilities designed to let operators manage, automate, and observe infrastructure from a single control plane. At its core Systems Manager centralizes tasks you would otherwise perform with many tools: starting interactive sessions, running scripts across many instances, applying OS and application patches, aggregating inventory and compliance, and surfacing operational work items. The SSM Agent on each managed instance provides the link between the cloud service and the host. Without that agent or the required IAM permissions, many Systems Manager features cannot execute. A concrete example is automating a diagnostic script across 200 instances using Run Command: Systems Manager uses the agent to deliver and run the script, then collects outputs to CloudWatch or S3. A common misconception is to think Systems Manager replaces monitoring: it complements CloudWatch and CloudTrail by providing execution and remediation tied to operational data. Key takeaway: Systems Manager reduces manual, error-prone ad-hoc work by providing repeatable, auditable actions that you can control at scale. How might consolidating a handful of admin tasks into SSM reduce your mean time to resolution?

keyIdea.title: SSM purpose
keyIdea.text: Unify execution, access, patching, and operational aggregation so teams can act consistently and audibly across instances.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is AWS Systems Manager?
A consolidated suite for managing tasks like access, remote execution, patching, and aggregated operational insights.
  • SSM Agent connects managed instances to the service and enables commands and sessions.
  • SSM provides multiple capabilities: Session Manager, Run Command, Patch Manager, Explorer, and OpsCenter.
  • Outputs and logs can be sent to CloudWatch Logs or S3 for auditing and analysis.
Key Takeaway

SSM centralizes operational actions and visibility so you can automate and audit at scale.

Term cards
SSM Agent
Installed on hosts; required to run commands and sessions.
Session Manager
Interactive, auditable shell access without SSH.
Run Command
Execute scripts or commands across many instances.
Patch Manager
Scan and apply patches using baselines and windows.
Common misconception: SSM replaces CloudWatch for monitoring. It does not — it complements monitoring by enabling remediation and access tied to monitoring signals.

screens.title: SSM Agent and IAM Role Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Before you can use most Systems Manager capabilities the managed host must run the SSM Agent and the host must have an IAM role granting Systems Manager the permissions it needs. The SSM Agent is a lightweight service that polls the Systems Manager endpoints and executes requested actions such as running a shell script or starting an interactive session. On supported Amazon Linux images the agent is often preinstalled, but for other operating systems you must install and start it. The instance IAM role should include the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy or an equivalent set of permissions so the agent can authenticate and call the SSM A P I. A real-world example: if you try to start a Session Manager session and the agent is not running, the instance will not appear as a managed instance and the session will fail. A common mistake is to grant only minimal EC2 permissions but forget the SSM-managed permissions, leading to silent access failures. The key operational habit is to verify agent status and role permissions during provisioning so Systems Manager capabilities become available immediately when needed.

keyIdea.title: Agent + Role = Managed Instance
keyIdea.text: SSM Agent running and proper IAM permissions are prerequisites for sessions, commands, and patching to succeed.

content.html:
Prerequisite
SSM Agent and IAM Role
Confirm these before relying on SSM features.
  • SSM Agent must be installed and running on each managed instance.
  • Instance role should include AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore or equivalent permissions.
  • Without either, the instance will not register as a managed instance and features will fail silently.
Check example: sudo systemctl status amazon-ssm-agent — start it if stopped.
Concrete example
sudo systemctl status amazon-ssm-agent
# if inactive
sudo systemctl start amazon-ssm-agent
# verify in Systems Manager Fleet Manager that the instance appears as a managed instance
Key Takeaway

Provision instances so the agent and role are present to avoid manual remediation later.

screens.title: Session Manager: Secure, Auditable Interactive Shells
screens.narratorSegment: Session Manager provides an interactive shell into managed instances without requiring open inbound ports or distributed SSH keys. Instead of adding systems to a bastion host or managing key pairs, you grant IAM permissions and start sessions through the Systems Manager console or A P I. Sessions are logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3, giving an audit trail of commands and output. For example, after confirming the SSM Agent is running and the instance role is correct, you can start a session from the console and run diagnostics like checking disk space or listing root. A concrete verification example: run a few commands such as checking filesystem usage and processes, then end the session and review the session history to confirm commands were recorded. A frequent misconception is that Session Manager bypasses IAM controls — in fact it relies on IAM to control who can start sessions and which targets they may access. Key takeaway: session-based access reduces attack surface and provides an auditable record for compliance. Which existing SSH workflows could you simplify first with Session Manager? Session Manager: Secure, Auditable Interactive Shells means removes ssh keys and open ports while keeping a complete session audit for security and compliance.. In practical terms, replace ssh by using browser-based sessions and central logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Interactive Access
Session Manager
Start secure, auditable interactive shells without SSH.
  • Use IAM to grant session permissions — no SSH keys to manage.
  • Session data is logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3 for auditing.
  • Works with EC2 and on-premises servers that run the SSM Agent.
Common Mistake

Assuming Session Manager bypasses IAM. It enforces IAM for who can start sessions and which instances are available.

Guided terminal example
# Example interactive checks you might run after connecting via Session Manager
ls -l /
df -h
ps aux | grep httpd
# then exit the session with the exit command and review Session history in Systems Manager
Key Takeaway

Session Manager simplifies access and gives a complete audit trail of interactive troubleshooting steps.

screens.title: Session Manager vs SSH
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing Session Manager and SSH helps clarify when to prefer one over the other. With SSH you typically need inbound port access, key distribution, or a bastion host. SSH sessions are powerful and familiar, but managing keys at scale and opening ports increases attack surface. Session Manager removes the need for inbound ports and distributed keys by using the SSM Agent and IAM-based permissions to authorize sessions. A concrete contrast: when a developer needs temporary access to investigate a crash in production, Session Manager lets you start a browser-based shell with audit logs captured centrally. With SSH you might provision a key or route through a bastion, and those steps increase operational friction and risk. A misconception is thinking Session Manager cannot provide the same shell utilities — it provides a standard shell and records the session. Key takeaway: prefer Session Manager for secure, auditable access in production environments; SSH remains useful for specific workflows where direct TCP tunnels are required. Session Manager vs SSH means session manager reduces risk and administrative overhead compared to ssh, especially for production troubleshooting.. In practical terms, contrast access models and key security implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
Session Manager vs SSH
Session Manager
No inbound ports, IAM-based access, session logs to CloudWatch/S3, browser-based shell.
SSH
Key management, open ports or bastion hosts, familiar tooling for tunnels and SCP.
Misconception: Session Manager lacks shell features — it provides a standard shell and supports common admin commands.
Concrete scenario
A production incident occurs: use Session Manager to open an auditable shell, gather diagnostics, and attach commands to an OpsItem. This avoids exposing a public SSH port and creates an audit record for compliance.
Key Takeaway

Session Manager is the preferred production access method when security and auditability matter most.

screens.title: Run Command: Execute Scripts Across a Fleet
screens.narratorSegment: Run Command lets you execute scripts and commands remotely on one or many managed instances using SSM Documents. You can use built-in documents such as AWS-RunShellScript or author custom documents in JSON or YAML. A practical example from the lab: select AWS-RunShellScript and provide commands like checking disk usage. The command runs through the SSM Agent and can send output to CloudWatch Logs or an S3 bucket for auditing and review. Run Command is ideal for ad-hoc diagnostics or one-off configuration changes. Remember to use target selection carefully and to test your document on a small set of instances before broad rollout. A common mistake is running a command with overly broad permissions or without a staged rollout; always specify MaxConcurrency and MaxErrors to limit the blast radius so a bad script does not impact your entire fleet. Key takeaway: Run Command gives you controlled, auditable remote execution — useful for diagnostics and repeatable operational tasks. Run Command: Execute Scripts Across a Fleet means execute scripts securely at scale using ssm documents and capture outputs centrally for auditing.. In practical terms, use ssm documents like aws-runshellscript to run diagnostics or installs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: Execute scripts securely at scale using SSM Documents and capture outputs centrally for auditing.

content.html:
Remote Execution
Run Command
Use SSM Documents to run scripts across selected targets and gather output for auditing.
  • Use built-in documents like AWS-RunShellScript for shell commands.
  • Configure output destinations: CloudWatch Logs or S3 for later review.
  • Always test commands on a small subset before large rollouts.
Command example
# Example Run Command content for AWS-RunShellScript
commands:
  - df -h
  - echo "Disk usage collected successfully."
# Target: manually selected instances
# Output: optionally to an S3 bucket or CloudWatch Logs
Key Takeaway

Use Run Command for controlled, auditable execution and configure outputs for later analysis.

screens.title: Controlling Rollouts: MaxConcurrency and MaxErrors
screens.narratorSegment: When executing commands across many instances it’s essential to limit the blast radius. Run Command provides two parameters to help: MaxConcurrency controls how many instances run the command at the same time, and MaxErrors defines how many failures are permitted before the operation stops. For instance, if you have 50 instances and set MaxConcurrency to 10 and MaxErrors to 3, the system will only run the command on up to 10 instances concurrently and will abort the run if more than three instances return errors. This staging approach lets you verify behavior on an initial batch before wider rollout. A common error is leaving MaxConcurrency unconstrained or setting MaxErrors too high and unintentionally allowing a bad script to affect most of your fleet. A practical example is deploying a package: test on one or two instances, then a small batch, and monitor outputs sent to CloudWatch logs. Key takeaway: use controlled concurrency and error limits to safely automate fleet operations. Controlling Rollouts: MaxConcurrency and MaxErrors means use maxconcurrency and maxerrors to stage operations and stop when failures indicate a problem.. In practical terms, prevent widespread failures by staging run command executions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Best Practice
MaxConcurrency & MaxErrors
Parameters to limit concurrent execution and acceptable failures.
  1. Set MaxConcurrency to limit how many instances run in parallel.
  2. Set MaxErrors to define failure tolerance before stopping the run.
  3. Stage rollouts: test on small groups, then increase concurrency if results are healthy.
Scenario
Deploying a new release to 50 instances: set MaxConcurrency to 10 and MaxErrors to 3 so only 10 update simultaneously and the run stops when more than three fail.
Common Mistake

Not specifying concurrency or error limits can lead to widespread issues from a single bad command.

screens.title: Patch Manager and Patch Baselines
screens.narratorSegment: Patch Manager automates scanning and applying operating system and application patches across managed instances. You define a patch baseline that lists which patches are approved for installation and which are rejected; Patch Manager uses that baseline during scans and patch operations. Integrating with the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document lets you apply patches programmatically or on a schedule. Use maintenance windows to ensure patches are applied during non-peak hours to minimize disruption. A concrete example: create a baseline that approves security updates but excludes specific driver updates, then schedule a maintenance window during off-hours to apply those patches. A common misconception is thinking patching should be manual for every host — at scale, automation reduces risk and human error. Key takeaway: maintain and review baselines regularly and schedule windows so patches are applied consistently without surprise downtime. Patch Manager and Patch Baselines means patch manager applies approved patches per baseline in scheduled windows to reduce manual effort and risk.. In practical terms, automate patch scans and installations with approved baselines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll explore AWS Systems Manager — a unified set of capabilities that help you manage and troubleshoot EC2 instances and on-premises servers at scale. Systems Manager brings together secure interactive access, remote command execution, automated patching, and centralized operational views so you can shorten time-to-resolution and maintain compliance across many instances. You will learn why having the SSM Agent and correct IAM role is a prerequisite, how Session Manager removes the need for SSH keys and open inbound ports, and how Run Command and Patch Manager let you perform repeatable operations safely across a fleet. We’ll also cover Explorer and OpsCenter, which aggregate operational data and surface actionable work items. As you follow this module, think about a fleet you manage: replacing ad-hoc SSH troubleshooting with Session Manager and centralized runbooks reduces risk and creates an audit trail. By the end you'll know which Systems Manager capability to choose for common operational tasks, how to limit blast radius with MaxConcurrency and MaxErrors, and how to keep systems patched in a maintenance window. Which operational pain point would you solve first with Systems Manager?

Over the next screens you'll gain four practical competencies that align with real SysOps tasks. First, you'll understand the capabilities of Systems Manager — what it consolidates and the practical limits of agent-based management. Knowing this helps you choose when to rely on SSM versus raw SSH or other tools. Second, you'll be able to use Session Manager to start secure, auditable interactive sessions that remove the need for inbound SSH and key distribution; this matters because it reduces attack surface and eases compliance reporting. Third, you'll learn to execute remote scripts and diagnostics using Run Command safely across many instances, including how to control concurrency and failures to limit blast radius. Fourth, you'll apply Patch Manager patterns to scan and apply operating system updates using patch baselines and maintenance windows, reducing manual effort and risk. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic and a milestone marker so you can verify hands-on competence as you progress. By mastering these objectives you will cut incident resolution time and increase operational consistency across your managed fleet.

These additional objectives focus on visibility and readiness. First, you'll learn how Explorer aggregates operational summaries across accounts and regions so you can prioritize high-impact issues quickly. This matters because a single dashboard reduces context switching between consoles and surfaces patch compliance and OpsItem counts. Second, you'll learn to use OpsCenter to investigate and track OpsItems, attach runbooks, and assign tasks so a team can resolve incidents efficiently. The practical skill here is turning alerts into tracked work items and knowing when to apply a runbook versus manual intervention. Third, you will practice verifying the SSM Agent and IAM role prerequisites with simple checks. Confirming the agent and role are present keeps systems manageable and prevents surprises when you try to start sessions or run commands. Fourth, you'll follow a hands-on activity to start a session, run a diagnostic command, and inspect logs — that lab builds confidence and provides a repeatable verification pattern. Each objective includes a milestone so you can mark readiness after completing the hands-on steps.

AWS Systems Manager is a suite of capabilities designed to let operators manage, automate, and observe infrastructure from a single control plane. At its core Systems Manager centralizes tasks you would otherwise perform with many tools: starting interactive sessions, running scripts across many instances, applying OS and application patches, aggregating inventory and compliance, and surfacing operational work items. The SSM Agent on each managed instance provides the link between the cloud service and the host. Without that agent or the required IAM permissions, many Systems Manager features cannot execute. A concrete example is automating a diagnostic script across 200 instances using Run Command: Systems Manager uses the agent to deliver and run the script, then collects outputs to CloudWatch or S3. A common misconception is to think Systems Manager replaces monitoring: it complements CloudWatch and CloudTrail by providing execution and remediation tied to operational data. Key takeaway: Systems Manager reduces manual, error-prone ad-hoc work by providing repeatable, auditable actions that you can control at scale. How might consolidating a handful of admin tasks into SSM reduce your mean time to resolution?

Before you can use most Systems Manager capabilities the managed host must run the SSM Agent and the host must have an IAM role granting Systems Manager the permissions it needs. The SSM Agent is a lightweight service that polls the Systems Manager endpoints and executes requested actions such as running a shell script or starting an interactive session. On supported Amazon Linux images the agent is often preinstalled, but for other operating systems you must install and start it. The instance IAM role should include the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy or an equivalent set of permissions so the agent can authenticate and call the SSM A P I. A real-world example: if you try to start a Session Manager session and the agent is not running, the instance will not appear as a managed instance and the session will fail. A common mistake is to grant only minimal EC2 permissions but forget the SSM-managed permissions, leading to silent access failures. The key operational habit is to verify agent status and role permissions during provisioning so Systems Manager capabilities become available immediately when needed.

Session Manager provides an interactive shell into managed instances without requiring open inbound ports or distributed SSH keys. Instead of adding systems to a bastion host or managing key pairs, you grant IAM permissions and start sessions through the Systems Manager console or A P I. Sessions are logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3, giving an audit trail of commands and output. For example, after confirming the SSM Agent is running and the instance role is correct, you can start a session from the console and run diagnostics like checking disk space or listing root. A concrete verification example: run a few commands such as checking filesystem usage and processes, then end the session and review the session history to confirm commands were recorded. A frequent misconception is that Session Manager bypasses IAM controls — in fact it relies on IAM to control who can start sessions and which targets they may access. Key takeaway: session-based access reduces attack surface and provides an auditable record for compliance. Which existing SSH workflows could you simplify first with Session Manager? In practical terms, replace ssh by using browser-based sessions and central logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparing Session Manager and SSH helps clarify when to prefer one over the other. With SSH you typically need inbound port access, key distribution, or a bastion host. SSH sessions are powerful and familiar, but managing keys at scale and opening ports increases attack surface. Session Manager removes the need for inbound ports and distributed keys by using the SSM Agent and IAM-based permissions to authorize sessions. A concrete contrast: when a developer needs temporary access to investigate a crash in production, Session Manager lets you start a browser-based shell with audit logs captured centrally. OpsCenter centralizes operational work items called OpsItems. These can be created automatically by services like CloudWatch Alarms or AWS Config, or created manually by operators. Each OpsItem captures details about the affected resource, severity, and suggested remediation steps. OpsCenter enables assignment to team members, adding notes, and attaching SSM Automation runbooks to automate resolution steps. For example, a recurring alert about disk saturation can create an OpsItem; you investigate, run diagnostics using Run Command, then attach a documented automation to free space or notify owners. A common mistake is treating OpsCenter as merely an alert list; its value comes from tracking lifecycle, assigning ownership, and automating resolution via runbooks. Key takeaway: convert alerts into OpsItems and use runbooks so remediation is consistent, documented, and repeatable. Let's distill the chapter into three core concepts to carry forward. First, AWS Systems Manager centralizes operational control: access, remote execution, patching, and aggregated visibility. Think of it as the operational toolbox that sits alongside CloudWatch and CloudTrail. Second, the SSM Agent plus the correct IAM role are prerequisites — without them, managed instances won’t be reachable by SSM features. Verifying agent status and instance role is the simplest preventative measure. Third, choose the right capability for the job: Session Manager for secure interactive access with auditing; Run Command for remote scripted execution with controlled concurrency and error limits; Patch Manager for automated patching via baselines and maintenance windows. These concepts reduce manual effort and increase auditability. As you practice the hands-on steps, remember to test on small groups and configure outputs so you always have an audit trail of what ran and why.

A compact quick reference will help you recall the most actionable points: first, use Session Manager in place of SSH for production troubleshooting to eliminate inbound ports and ensure sessions are logged. Second, when executing across many hosts, always set MaxConcurrency and MaxErrors in Run Command so a faulty script stops before widespread impact. Third, automate patching through Patch Manager with defined baselines and maintenance windows to reduce manual updates and increase consistency. As a final practice tip, always configure output destinations for commands and sessions so you have a persistent audit trail in CloudWatch or S3. These small habits — preferring Session Manager, staging Run Command rollouts, and scheduling patch windows — will materially reduce risk and time spent on firefighting.
